bibl.title: Auditory, visual, and cross-modal negative priming

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: To our knowledge, the present experiment is the first to demonstrate negative priming, using the same experimental task, with visual and auditory stimuli and also across these two modalities.

span.label: negative priming
span.quote: Negative priming refers to the phenomenon that a reaction to a stimulus can be slowed down or more likely to be in error if the stimulus has recently been ignored.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Auditory, visual, and cross-modal negative priming was investigated using a task in which participants judged whether stimuli were animals or musical instruments.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: presenting a stimulus in one modality automatically activates its features in the other modality, so an ignored sound can prime (and slow) a later picture
span.quote: Second, the presentation of a stimulus in one modality may automatically activate features in other modalities.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: distractor inhibition is applied only to distractors that interfere: nonconflict distractors need no inhibition, hence no later cost
span.quote: It could be assumed that nonconflict prime distractors do not interfere with the prime reaction, so that they need not be inhibited.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the probe target retrieves the earlier prime episode, which carries a 'no response was made' tag that conflicts with the current requirement to respond
span.quote: Within the episodic retrieval account, negative priming may be caused by the probe target’s cuing the retrieval of the perceptually similar prime display in which the distractor representation contains the information that no response was (to be) made to that stimulus.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: acoustic traces of ignored sounds persist in a long auditory store better than visual distractor traces persist in visual short-term memory, producing facilitation that offsets or reverses the negative-priming cost
span.quote: It seems possible that the acoustic aspects of auditory distractor representations are maintained more efficiently in a “long auditory store” (see Cowan, 1984) than the perceptual aspects of the representations of visual distractors are maintained in visual short-term memory.

span.label: Prime conflict is unavoidably confounded with whether the prime and probe responses alternate or repeat, which makes the key finding ambiguous in principle.
span.quote: Although this unavoidable confound renders the interpretation of the present finding ambiguous in principle, we believe that the conflict/nonconflict nature of the primes, and not the prime–probe response alternation/repetition, determined the observed pattern of performance.

span.label: The unexpected positive priming after nonconflict primes in the auditory-auditory condition can only be accounted for speculatively.
span.quote: We can only speculate about the underlying mechanisms.

span.label: The positive priming found on nonconflict prime trials in the auditory-auditory condition was not predicted.
span.quote: The positive priming on nonconflict prime trials in the auditory–auditory condition was unexpected.

span.label: negative priming
span.quote: Negative priming refers to the phenomenon that a reaction to a stimulus can be slowed down or more likely to be in error if the stimulus has recently been ignored

span.label: conflict
span.quote: Negative priming was observed only after conflict, but not after nonconflict, primes. Note, however, that prime and probe responses necessarily changed in the former case

span.label: distractor inhibition
span.quote: If this position is accepted, the observed data pattern is most easily explained within the distractor inhibition (Tipper, 1985; Tipper & Cranston, 1985) and the episodic retrieval accounts of negative priming

span.label: episodic retrieval
span.quote: Within the episodic retrieval account, negative priming may be caused by the probe target’s cuing the retrieval of the perceptually similar prime display in which the distractor representation contains the information that no response was (to be) made to that stimulus. This nonresponse information conflicts with the requirement to react to the prime target

span.label: A PRIME THAT HURTS BECAUSE IT WAS IGNORED, WHICH IS A RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN PRIME AND TARGET THAT NOTHING ELSE IN THIS CORPUS HAS. `A reaction to a stimulus can be SLOWED DOWN or more likely to be in error IF THE STIMULUS HAS RECENTLY BEEN IGNORED.` The manipulation is an INSTRUCTION TO DISREGARD, so what carries over is the act of suppression. **And it is a cost, not a benefit** - the second counterexample tonight to the standard `improvement` definition Minton2017 strikes out (Q-780), after Huang2018's interference effect
span.quote: Negative priming refers to the phenomenon that a reaction to a stimulus can be slowed down or more likely to be in error if the stimulus has recently been ignored

span.label: AND IGNORING IS NOT ENOUGH - IT HAD TO HAVE BEEN COMPETING: `Negative priming was observed ONLY AFTER CONFLICT, but not after nonconflict, primes.` The ignored item must have called for a DIFFERENT response from the attended one. So the phenomenon is not about suppression in general but about suppression under competition, and a design that ignores an irrelevant stimulus with no competing response should find nothing. **Another `only when`, and the condition is a property of the RELATION between the two primes rather than of either one**
span.quote: Negative priming was observed only after conflict, but not after nonconflict, primes. Note, however, that prime and probe responses necessarily changed in the former case

span.label: THE AUTHORS MARK EXACTLY HOW MUCH OF THEIR CONCLUSION RESTS ON SOMETHING THEY CANNOT TEST: `ALTHOUGH THIS UNAVOIDABLE CONFOUND renders the interpretation of the present finding AMBIGUOUS IN PRINCIPLE, WE BELIEVE that the conflict/nonconflict nature of the primes, and not the prime-probe response alternation/repetition, determined the observed pattern.` Then: `IF THIS POSITION IS ACCEPTED, the observed data pattern is most easily explained within...` **Four markers in three sentences - unavoidable, ambiguous in principle, we believe, if this position is accepted - and everything downstream is explicitly conditional on the belief.** The confound is structural: conflict primes necessarily change the response, so the two cannot be separated by any version of this design
span.quote: Although this unavoidable confound renders the interpretation of the present finding ambiguous in principle, we believe that the conflict/nonconflict nature of the primes, and not the prime–probe response alternation/repetition, determined the observed pattern of performance

span.label: AN UNEXPECTED RESULT ADMITTED AS UNEXPLAINED: `The positive priming on nonconflict prime trials in the auditory-auditory condition WAS UNEXPECTED. WE CAN ONLY SPECULATE about the underlying mechanisms.` The effect ran the WRONG WAY in one cell - facilitation where the paper predicts none - and it gets a paragraph of candidate explanations, each marked as speculation, rather than a footnote. **A record that stored only the headline `negative priming after conflict primes` would lose a cell that contradicts the framework**
span.quote: The positive priming on nonconflict prime trials in the auditory–auditory condition was unexpected. We can only speculate about the underlying mechanisms

span.label: THREE ACCOUNTS ARE TESTED AGAINST THE SAME PATTERN AND ONE OF THEM HAS TO BE PATCHED: distractor inhibition and episodic retrieval both accommodate the conflict result, but for the temporal discrimination account `IN ORDER TO EXPLAIN THE LACK OF NEGATIVE PRIMING ON NONCONFLICT TRIALS, THE TEMPORAL DISCRIMINATION ACCOUNT MUST BE EXTENDED.` Two alternative extensions are then offered, both hypothetical. **The paper reports which theory needs extra machinery to survive its data**, which is a more useful thing to record than which theory it prefers
span.quote: In order to explain the lack of negative priming on nonconflict trials, the temporal discrimination account must be extended

span.label: replicates → Driver and Baylis (1993)
span.quote: This demonstration is consonant with the finding of auditory-to-visual negative priming by Driver and Baylis (1993).

span.label: extends → Driver and Baylis (1993, Experiment 1)
span.quote: To our knowledge, only Driver and Baylis (1993, Experiment 1) have investigated cross-modal negative priming, but only the auditory-tovisual side of it.

span.label: conflict —causes→ negative priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — **THE `ONLY AFTER` IS THE CLAIM AND IT IS IN THE QUOTE.** Weight 0.85 rather than higher because of the confound the authors name themselves: conflict primes NECESSARILY change the response between prime and probe, so this edge and `response alternation causes negative priming` are not separable by any version of this design. The paper says so - `ambiguous in principle` - and the third sense carries it.
span.quote: Negative priming was observed only after conflict, but not after nonconflict, primes. Note, however, that prime and probe responses necessarily changed in the former case

span.label: distractor inhibition —contrasted-with→ episodic retrieval
span.note: differs in: WHETHER ANYTHING IS SUPPRESSED AT ALL. Inhibition says the ignored item is actively damped and is still damped when it returns. Episodic retrieval says nothing is suppressed - the probe RETRIEVES the earlier display, which carries a tag that no response was to be made, and that tag conflicts with responding now. **Same prediction for the conflict result, opposite claims about what is in the head between the two trials** · strength of the relation: 0.9 — Both accounts survive this paper's data, and the span carries both statements so a reader meets the alternative rather than the winner. Weight 0.9: the paper states both as live options in the same paragraph and picks neither.
span.quote: If this position is accepted, the observed data pattern is most easily explained within the distractor inhibition (Tipper, 1985; Tipper & Cranston, 1985) and the episodic retrieval accounts of negative priming

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Error differences were significantly above zero for the NC/NC and the NC/C trial types [t(70) 5 2.71 and 2.00, respectively], and they were significantly below zero for the C/C trial type [t(70) 5 22.21].

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A 4 3 2 analysis of variance with presentation condition as a between-subjects variable and probe type as a withinsubjects variable showed that the probe type variable failed to reach the conventional level of significance

span.label: effect size (Cohen's dz)
span.quote: and in the auditory–auditory dz 5 0.55, and t(70) 5 24.54, condition [t(70) 5 24.60, dz 5 0.54, respectively].

span.label: significance level (alpha)
span.quote: The level of a was set to .05 for all analyses.

span.label: standard error
span.quote: The error bars depict the standard errors of the means.

span.label: Negative priming appeared only when the attended and ignored members of the prime pair called for different responses; nonconflict primes produced none.
span.quote: Negative priming was observed, but only if the attended and the ignored primes evoked different responses.

span.label: The conflict-only pattern of negative priming held for visual stimuli, for auditory stimuli, and in both cross-modal directions (auditory-to-visual and visual-to-auditory).
span.quote: This pattern—negative priming after conflict, but not after nonconflict, primes—was demonstrated with visual stimuli and replicated with auditory stimuli, as well as across modalities, both auditory to visual and visual to auditory.

span.label: Cross-modal negative priming was about equally strong in both directions, so the effect is not specific to the auditory-to-visual switch previously reported.
span.quote: In addition, the present data show that auditory-to-visual and visual-toauditory negative priming is fairly symmetrical.

span.label: In the auditory-auditory condition, nonconflict-prime trials produced positive priming (faster responses to the previously ignored sound) instead of the null effect seen in the other three presentation conditions.
span.quote: In trials with nonconflict probes in the auditory–auditory condition, we observed positive priming, rather than no priming, as in the other presentation conditions.

span.label: Whether the probe pair itself was conflicting did not reliably change the size of negative priming.
span.quote: A 4 3 2 analysis of variance with presentation condition as a between-subjects variable and probe type as a withinsubjects variable showed that the probe type variable failed to reach the conventional level of significance

span.label: Collapsing across the conflict/nonconflict prime distinction would have shown significant negative priming in the visual-visual condition while falsely concluding there is none in the auditory-auditory condition, which may explain the near absence of published auditory negative-priming work.
span.quote: ignoring the conflict–nonconflict prime distinction would have led to the finding of significant negative priming in the visual–visual condition, but it would have led us to erroneously accept the null hypothesis of no negative priming in the auditory–auditory condition.

span.label: Probe responses were faster after visual than after auditory probes and slower after conflicting than after nonconflicting probes, while prime modality had no effect on probe speed.
span.quote: Most obviously, (1) probe reactions were faster after visual than after auditory probes (669 vs. 897 msec), whereas prime modality did not have an effect, and (2) probe reactions were slower following conflict, as opposed to nonconflict, probes (819 vs. 747 msec).

span.label: Because the ignored prime's response category was matched between ignored-repetition and control trials, the observed cross-modal effects cannot be explained by response-level information and must reflect stimulus identity.
span.quote: This implies that any performance differences between control and ignored repetition trials must be due to the stimulus identity and cannot be due to the response category associated with it.

span.label: negative priming
span.quote: Negative priming refers to the phenomenon that a reaction to a stimulus can be slowed down or more likely to be in error if the stimulus has recently been ignored.

span.label: conflict pair versus nonconflict pair
span.quote: Given two possible categories, the attended and the to-be-ignored stimuli of each pair could be from the same category and, thus, require the same response (nonconflict pair), or they could be from different categories and, thus, require different responses (conflict pair).

span.label: presentation condition (visual-visual, auditory-visual, visual-auditory, auditory-auditory)
span.quote: The independent variables were presentation condition (visual– visual, auditory– visual, visual–auditory, and auditory–auditory; between subjects) and trial type (NC/NC, NC/C, C/NC, and C/C; within subject).

span.label: trial type (conflict vs nonconflict prime crossed with conflict vs nonconflict probe)
span.term: trial type (conflict vs nonconflict prime crossed with conflict vs nonconflict probe)
span.quote: The independent variables were presentation condition (visual– visual, auditory– visual, visual–auditory, and auditory–auditory; between subjects) and trial type (NC/NC, NC/C, C/NC, and C/C; within subject).

span.label: probe reaction time
span.quote: Mean probe reaction times and error percentages as a function of presentation condition (visual–visual, auditory–visual, visual–auditory, and auditory–auditory; between subjects) and trial type (NC represents nonconflict primes/probes, C represents conflict primes/probes).

span.label: probe error percentage
span.quote: Mean probe reaction times and error percentages as a function of presentation condition (visual–visual, auditory–visual, visual–auditory, and auditory–auditory; between subjects) and trial type (NC represents nonconflict primes/probes, C represents conflict primes/probes).

span.label: response category of the ignored prime (held identical across ignored-repetition and matched control trials)
span.term: response category of the ignored prime (held identical across ignored-repetition and matched control trials)
span.quote: Also note that the response category of the ignored prime was always the same on an ignored repetition and its corresponding control trial.

span.label: probe stimulus pair (held identical between an ignored-repetition trial and its matching control trial)
span.term: probe stimulus pair (held identical between an ignored-repetition trial and its matching control trial)
span.quote: Furthermore, the probe stimulus pair was identical for an ignored repetition trial and its matching control trial, thus enabling an unequivocal comparison of the probe reactions.

span.label: spatial compatibility between tone location and response key (neutralised by sagittal key alignment)
span.term: spatial compatibility between tone location and response key (neutralised by sagittal key alignment)
span.quote: These keys were aligned sagittally so as to avoid spatial compatibility effects between the tone’s location and the required response.

span.label: 284 — number of undergraduate participants tested, 198 of them female, aged 18-58
span.quote: The participants were 284 undergraduate students (198 female), between 18 and 58 years of age (M 5 23).

span.label: 768 — number of prime-probe trials each participant completed
span.quote: The experiment consisted of 768 trials, each composed of a prime and a probe pair of stimuli.

span.label: 96 — number of prime/probe trials of each of the four trial types (NC/NC, NC/C, C/NC, C/C)
span.quote: There were 96 prime/probe trials of each type: NC/NC, NC/C, C/NC, and C/C.

span.label: 669 vs. 897 msec — mean probe reaction time after visual probes versus after auditory probes
span.quote: Most obviously, (1) probe reactions were faster after visual than after auditory probes (669 vs. 897 msec), whereas prime modality did not have an effect, and (2) probe reactions were slower following conflict, as opposed to nonconflict, probes (819 vs. 747 msec).

span.label: 819 vs. 747 msec — mean probe reaction time following conflict probes versus nonconflict probes
span.quote: Most obviously, (1) probe reactions were faster after visual than after auditory probes (669 vs. 897 msec), whereas prime modality did not have an effect, and (2) probe reactions were slower following conflict, as opposed to nonconflict, probes (819 vs. 747 msec).

span.label: 252 msec — size of the negative priming effect in the auditory-auditory condition, the largest of the four presentation conditions (the PDF extraction renders the minus sign as a leading 2, i.e. -52 msec, followed by -27, -26 and -18 msec)
span.quote: Descriptively, the effect seems to have been largest for the auditory–auditory condition (252 msec), followed by the visual–visual condition (227 msec), the visual–auditory condition (226 msec), and the auditory–visual condition (218 msec).

span.label: 2 msec — the overall auditory-auditory priming effect when conflict and nonconflict prime trials are pooled - negligible and in the positive direction, which is why pooling hides the effect
span.quote: The effect was only 2 msec and in the wrong direction.

span.label: 725 vs. 966 msec — mean prime reaction time after visual primes versus after auditory primes
span.quote: Prime reactions were faster after visual than after auditory primes (725 vs. 966 msec).
